title: Photoelectric effect
examples: What happens if I shine a very dim light on metal?
Does the color of light change how much electricity I get?
Is the brightness of the light more important than its color?

explain.say: Today we explore the photoelectric effect. Say this with me: the photoelectric effect.
The photoelectric effect shows light ejecting electrons from metal. This happens when light shines on a metal surface.
The first key idea is the threshold frequency. This is the minimum light frequency needed to eject electrons. Below this frequency, no electrons are emitted.
Next we look at the energy relationship. The energy of the incoming photon equals the work function plus maximum kinetic energy. This is a core equation.
The second important concept is the relationship between frequency and energy. Higher frequency light means higher energy photons. This energy is what knocks out the electrons.
For a real-life example, imagine a solar panel. It uses the photoelectric effect to convert light into electricity. The light must have enough energy to excite the material.

draw.text: Solar panels convert light to electricity.

faq.q: Why does the color of light matter so much?
faq.a: The color relates to the frequency of the light. Different colors mean different frequencies, which determines the energy available to eject electrons.
asks: Does the wavelength determine the energy?
How does color affect the photoelectric effect?

faq.q: If I use a very bright light, will I get more electrons?
faq.a: No, the brightness relates to the intensity, not the energy per photon. Intensity only changes the number of photons, not their individual energy.
asks: Does intensity affect the maximum kinetic energy?
Why does brightness not increase the energy?

faq.a: The work function is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from a specific metal surface. It is a property of the metal.
asks: Is the work function constant for all metals?

faq.q: Can I use a low-frequency, high-intensity light source?
faq.a: No, if the frequency is below the threshold frequency, no electrons will be ejected, no matter how bright the light is.
asks: Does intensity overcome the threshold frequency?
What is the minimum requirement for electron emission?

faq.q: How is this different from heating a metal?
faq.a: Heating provides thermal energy, which causes vibrations. Light provides discrete packets of energy called photons, which interact differently.
asks: Is photoelectric effect the same as heat?
What is the difference between thermal and light energy?

facts: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency.
The work function ($\phi$) is the minimum energy needed to eject an electron.
The maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons depends only on the light's frequency.
Increasing the intensity increases the number of ejected electrons, not their energy.

quiz.say: If the incident light frequency is exactly the threshold frequency, what is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?
quiz.why: At the threshold frequency, the photon energy exactly matches the work function, leaving no excess energy for kinetic motion.

wrong.1: This suggests there is leftover energy, but at the threshold, all energy is used up.
wrong.2: This confuses the required energy ($\phi$) with the resulting kinetic energy.
wrong.3: This implies an unlimited amount of energy is available, which is incorrect for the minimum condition.

quiz.say: A metal requires $3.0 \times 10^{-19}$ joules to eject an electron. If light of frequency $5.0 \times 10^{14}$ hertz shines on it, what is the maximum kinetic energy?
quiz.why: We use $hf = \phi + KE{max}$. The excess energy is the kinetic energy, so $KE{max} = hf - \phi$.

wrong.0: This would only be correct if the frequency was exactly the threshold frequency.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes the kinetic energy is equal to the work function.
wrong.3: This forgets to subtract the energy used to overcome the work function.

quiz.say: If I double the intensity of the light, what happens to the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?
quiz.why: Maximum kinetic energy depends only on the frequency, not the intensity or brightness of the light source.

wrong.0: This suggests an inverse relationship that does not exist in this physical model.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes that more photons mean more energy per electron.
wrong.3: This confuses the total number of electrons with the energy of each individual electron.
